summary.text: A mid-ocean ridge is an underwater mountain system that forms along a divergent plate boundary, where the seafloor spreads apart.
As the plates separate, mantle rises and melts, and the magma erupts as lava that cools into new oceanic crust.
Most ridges are connected in one global system that is part of every ocean, making it the longest mountain range in the world.

items.prompt: Where is the longest mountain range on Earth?

options.label: Along the west side of South America
On the ocean floor, linking every ocean

items.explain: Most mid-ocean ridges are connected into one global system that is part of every ocean, making it the longest mountain range in the world, several times longer than the Andes.

items.prompt: A ship drills seafloor rock samples along a line heading away from a ridge's central axis. What pattern in the rocks' ages does it find?

options.label: They get younger farther from the axis
They get older farther from the axis
They are all the same age

items.explain: New crust forms at the axis, so the rocks are youngest there and grow older with distance from it.

items.prompt: Seafloor far from a ridge sits deeper than seafloor near it. Why?

options.label: Sediment piling on top pushes it down
As it cools, the material beneath grows denser

items.explain: Away from the ridge the plate cools and its mantle lithosphere thickens and becomes denser, so older seafloor sits deeper.

items.prompt: Roughly how fast do the plates move apart at mid-ocean ridges?
items.explain: Spreading rates range from about 10 to 200 mm per year.

items.prompt: How can scientists work out how fast a ridge has been spreading?

options.label: By timing how long fresh lava takes to cool
By counting earthquakes along the ridge each year
By measuring how warm the seawater is above it
By mapping magnetic patterns locked into the crust

items.explain: Cooling basalt records the direction of Earth's magnetic field, which has flipped at known intervals, so the pattern gives the crust's age and, with distance from the axis, the spreading rate.

items.prompt: One ridge widens by about 25 mm each year, another by about 120 mm each year. Which would you expect to have a large rift valley along its crest?
items.explain: Ridges spreading slower than 40 mm a year generally have large rift valleys, while those faster than 90 mm a year lack them.

pack.title: The Seam That Makes Seafloor
pack.question: How do mid-ocean ridges make new ocean floor?

beats.title: The Seam That Makes Seafloor
beats.hook: The longest mountain range in the world is underwater, and along its crest the ocean floor is constantly being renewed.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in the making of new seafloor in order.

items.label: Mantle rock wells up and melts
The lava cools into new oceanic crust

beats.explain: Mantle rises in response to the plates separating; the melt rises as magma between them, emerges as lava, and creates new crust as it cools.

beats.prompt: Basalt cools at a ridge while Earth's magnetic field points one way. Later, the field flips direction. What does that older basalt show now?
beats.explain: As basalt cools, it records the magnetic field's direction, so the crust keeps a record of the field over time, including its reversals.

choices.label: It still records the old direction
It loses its magnetic record entirely
choices.feedback: The record survives; that is what makes it useful for dating the crust.

choices.label: It flips to match the new field
choices.feedback: Tempting if rock acted like a compass needle, but once it cools the direction is locked in.

beats.prompt: Match each ridge feature to its description.
beats.explain: Spreading speed shapes a ridge: slow ridges like the Mid-Atlantic have steeper profiles, fast ones like the East Pacific Rise gentle ones, and the slowest are called ultraslow; old transform faults leave fracture zones on the flanks.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about seafloor depth is wrong. Which?

steps.text: New crust forms hot at the ridge axis.
Moving away, the plate cools and the mantle part beneath it thickens and gets denser.
Denser material floats higher, so old seafloor is shallower than young seafloor.
So seafloor depth is tied to the seafloor's age.

beats.explain: Older seafloor rests on denser material and is deeper, not shallower; depth on the ridge flanks is correlated with the seafloor's age.

beats.idea: Where plates pull apart, rising mantle melts and erupts as lava that becomes new crust, which cools, grows denser and sinks deeper as it moves away.

paragraphs.heading: Mountains on the seafloor
paragraphs.text: A mid-ocean ridge is a mountain system on the seafloor, built by plate tectonics. It marks a divergent plate boundary, where seafloor spreading widens an ocean basin. A ridge typically lies about 2,600 meters deep and rises some 2,000 meters above the deepest part of its basin. The first one found was the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which splits the North and South Atlantic basins, and its position gave these ridges their name, even though most spreading centers are not in the middle of their oceans.

paragraphs.heading: One chain around the world
paragraphs.text: Ridges across the globe are linked by plate boundaries, and their path over the ocean floor looks like the seam of a baseball. Most of them join into one global system, the Ocean Ridge, which runs through every ocean. Its continuous mountain range is 65,000 km long, several times longer than the Andes, and the whole ridge system adds up to 80,000 km.

paragraphs.heading: How new crust is made
paragraphs.text: As the plates pull apart, mantle rock wells up beneath them, producing new seafloor and new oceanic lithosphere, the crust plus the colder, denser part of the mantle that together form the plates. The melt rises as magma through the weak line between the plates, erupts as lava and cools into new crust. It melts by decompression, as rising solid mantle passes its solidus temperature. The magma crystallizes into a basalt called MORB, with gabbro below it in the lower crust, and hydrothermal vents fed by this heat are common along the ridges.

paragraphs.heading: Older seafloor sits deeper
paragraphs.text: The rocks are youngest along the ridge axis and get older the farther you go from it. Depth follows age: a good rule is that seafloor depth is proportional to the square root of its age. Near the axis, hot, low-density mantle props up the crust. Farther away the plate cools, its mantle layer thickens and grows denser, and so older seafloor rests deeper.

paragraphs.heading: Magnetic stripes keep time
paragraphs.text: Spreading rates are worked out by mapping magnetic patterns in the crust on both sides of a ridge. When basalt erupted at the axis cools, iron-titanium oxides in it lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field. Because the field has flipped at known times, the pattern of reversals dates the crust, and the age plus the distance from the axis gives the spreading rate. Rates run from about 10 to 200 mm a year.

paragraphs.heading: Slow ridges and fast ridges
paragraphs.text: Slow ridges, spreading under 40 mm a year like the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, have steep profiles, rift valleys up to 10–20 km wide and rugged crests with up to 1,000 m of relief. Fast ridges, over 90 mm a year like the East Pacific Rise, have gentle profiles and no rift valleys. The North Atlantic spreads at about 25 mm a year and the Pacific at 80–145 mm, and the highest known rate, over 200 mm a year, was on the East Pacific Rise in the Miocene. Ridges slower than 20 mm a year, such as the Gakkel Ridge in the Arctic, are called ultraslow.
